extracted.intended_audience: novelists, students of fiction, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying principles for writing and evaluating novels (form, time, point of view, character treatment, and method). Focus is on how a novelist shapes material to achieve unity, truth, and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination of distance / scale
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination of distance is everywhere ... not only in a free prospect, where sight is lost, but on any river-bank, where the course of the stream lies across a continent, or on the edge of a wood, whence the forest stretches round the curve of the globe. The horizon of a Russian story would naturally be vague and vast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a sense of large scale by implying continuity beyond the page: evoke horizons, uninterrupted prospects or the sense that the world continues past the scene. Contrast examples: Tolstoy creates an 'ample vision' opening in every direction; Dostoevsky achieves scale by shutting off natural day and concentrating inward. Anti-pattern: isolating a patch of setting so tightly that the world feels cut off and unnaturally small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of space and daylight
rubrics_metrics.description: The continuity of space and of daylight ... so necessary to the motive of the book, is rendered in War and Peace with absolute mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To suggest an expansive world, maintain continuity of physical space and light across scenes so readers feel a continuous environment. This can be accomplished not primarily by description but by giving characters latitude of movement and by implying daylight and space that extend beyond immediate scenes. Lack of such continuity can shrink the novel's horizon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom and latitude of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: He manages to give them such freedom, such an obvious latitude of movement in the open world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be written so they seem to have lives beyond the book's boundaries — free to move and act in the larger world. This is not simply a multiplication of names or detailed description, but a method of presentation that implies autonomy. Anti-pattern: overly authorial containment that makes characters feel puppeted or entirely confined to textual incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ordinary experience as foundation of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy seems to look squarely at the same world as other people, and only to make so much more of it than other people by the direct force of his genius ... His experience comes from the same quarter as ours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One effective method is to ground exceptional fiction in the familiar and everyday — observe common facts from a fully attentive stance. The writer's extra absorption and 'plastic imagination' transforms ordinary material into profound depiction. Contrast with writers who create a wholly otherworldly vantage point; both can work but produce different effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the passage of time (form of time)
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of time is to be represented, and that is something more than to represent its contents in their order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novel whose subject is time must make the movement of time perceptible structurally: the build, lines and masses of the book should express duration and change, not merely place facts in sequence. Avoid simply announcing 'years have fled'; the shape of the narrative must embody temporal flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double effect of time: steady progression and cyclical curve
rubrics_metrics.description: The double effect of time — its uninterrupted lapse, and the cycle of which the chosen stretch is a segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When time is central, represent both the steady, quiet slipping of days (small-scale change visible in faces, gestures, thought) and the larger arc or cycle (rise and fall, a generation's curve). A novel may need to show both the incremental passage and the sense that the period is part of a larger circulating sweep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency through aging and change
rubrics_metrics.description: They ... are always the people we know, the same as ever, and yet changing and changing ... Their mutability never hides their sameness, their consistency shows and endures through their disintegration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should evolve in ways consistent with their nature and circumstances: they change because of clashes with conditions, but retain an underlying unity of personality. This makes growth credible and supports long-term arcs (e.g., youth to middle age). Anti-pattern: arbitrary or inconsistent shifts that break reader belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative unity / design (moral in design)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral of it all — what of that? Tolstoy has shown us a certain length of time's journey, but to what end has he shown it? ... The moral is in its design, and without design the scattered scenes will make no picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novel needs an organizing design or purpose so scenes cohere into a discernible effect or 'moral'. Chapters and episodes should collate toward a central reason for their juxtaposition; otherwise the book risks appearing rambling or inconclusive. Anti-pattern: vacillation of intention that prevents the book's parts from announcing a single effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of material — avoid wasted life
rubrics_metrics.description: At any moment great masses of that life are being wasted, turned to no account; and the result is not merely negative, for ... the wasted life ... is dividing and weakening the effect of the picture created out of the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material that does not serve the book's design weakens the overall effect. Ensure episodes, characters, and incidents contribute—directly or by contrast—to the central subject. Trim or reshape abundant life so the profusion supports rather than dilutes the intended picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixing the subject before choosing method
rubrics_metrics.description: For my particular purpose ... there is no such book as [Bovary]; for it is a novel in which the subject stands firm and determined, so that it may be possible to consider the manner of its treatment with undivided attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the subject is sharply fixed, the novelist can choose and execute method precisely. Uncertain or shifting subjects invite wandering methods and an incoherent result. Flaubert's Madame Bovary serves as an example of subject-clarity enabling controlled method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing rather than mere statement (image over argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is not a row of facts, it is a single image; the facts have no validity in themselves, they are nothing until they have been used. The art of fiction does not begin until the novelist thinks of his story as a matter to be shown, to be so exhibited that it will tell itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move beyond reporting facts or assembling an 'argument' — shape facts so they produce an image or effect. The novelist selects and arranges detail to make the story 'tell itself' rather than relying on external attestation or summary. Anti-pattern: treating a novel as an official report or simple chronicle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of information to serve the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The way in which they are presented will entirely depend on the particular subject that Flaubert sees in them; until this is apparent the method cannot be criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose which facts to include or omit in light of the book's chosen subject and effect. Presentation decisions (what to narrate, what to dramatize, what to summarize) should be governed by the intended meaning; inconsistency indicates a mismatch between subject and method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intervention: when to supply background or interiority
rubrics_metrics.description: There comes a juncture at which, for some reason, it is necessary for us to know more than we could have made out by simply looking and listening. Flaubert ... must intervene with his superior knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authorial narration to supply past facts, context, or inner life when the dramatic scene cannot convey them. Balance such interventions with scenes that let events and dialogue demonstrate meaning; choose moments for omniscient commentary deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view: scenic vs panoramic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Are we placed before a particular scene ... ? Or are we surveying their lives from a height, participating in the privilege of the novelist — sweeping their history with a wide range of vision and absorbing a general effect? ... a 'scenic' and a 'panoramic' presentation of a story expresses an intelligible antithesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to present episodes up close (scenic) or to adopt a broad, time-spanning view (panoramic). Both can be used within a book but be aware of transitions and their effects on pacing and reader perspective. Sudden or unmoored shifts confuse the relation between reader, characters, and authorial stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial voice and impersonality (voice through self or character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the author is talking with his own voice, sometimes he is talking through one of the people in the book ... The famous 'impersonality' of Flaubert ... lies only in the greater tact with which they express their feelings—dramatizing them, embodying them in living form, instead of stating them directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage the degree of explicit authorial presence: speak directly, or dramatize judgments through characters' perceptions. 'Impersonality' is achieved by embodying the author's judgement in scenes and characters rather than explicit commentary. Be explicit about shifts between authorial language and character-filtered language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial vs dramatic treatment of scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a pictorial manner of treating the matter ... and there is also a dramatic. ... The thing is 'scenic,' ... but there it is all bathed in the climate of Emma's mood ... The scene is pictorially treated. ... This scene ... is rendered on the whole ... from Emma's point of view ... but the facts of the scene are well to the fore ... It is a scene which might be put upon the stage ... To receive the force of the contrast the reader has only to see and hear, to be present while the hour passes; and the author places him there accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to render an episode pictorially (filtering it through a character's mood, atmosphere, and internal coloration) or dramatically/objectively (foregrounding observable facts and dialogue). Pictorial treatment emphasizes interior response; dramatic treatment foregrounds action and objective detail. Mixing is possible but must be handled with craft to preserve intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious use of interiority / access to consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: He ... enters their consciousness, and describes the train of sentiment that passes there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When necessary, enter characters' minds to reveal motives, feelings, or past that the scene cannot show. Use interior access sparingly and where it heightens understanding; overuse can reduce dramatic immediacy or create authorial intrusiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of scope: large panorama vs finely controlled study
rubrics_metrics.description: For a sight of the large and general masses in which a novel takes shape, War and Peace seemed to promise more than another; but something a great deal more finely controlled is to be looked for ... Flaubert’s Madame Bovary ... is a novel in which the subject stands firm and determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose scope with intent: an expansive panoramic novel requires methods that sustain breadth (continuous space, many lives), while a concentrated study demands tight control of subject and method. Each has virtues; mismatch of scope and method creates incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain representative character when theme requires it
rubrics_metrics.description: It has entirely dropped the representative character which it wore at the beginning and is to pick up again at the end. Tolstoy has forgotten about this; partly he has been too much engrossed in his historical picture ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character is intended to be representative of a broader social or thematic idea, keep that representative aspect in view through the work. Allowing the narrative to shift modes and lose that representative function can undermine thematic coherence. Reconcile historical or other detours with the character's intended role.
